rounds.proof_sketch: blockDim.y=1 for 1D block, so shared_sum starts at shared_mem[1] instead of shared_mem[256]. The overlap destroys shared_max[1..255], but only shared_max[0] (the final max at shared_mem[0]) is needed after max reduction. shared_sum[0..255] maps to contiguous shared_mem[1..256], allowing correct sum reduction. The algorithm's synchronization barriers ensure proper ordering.
rounds.survival_reason: The mutation changes the base offset of shared_sum from 256 to 1, creating an overlap between shared_max and shared_sum arrays. However, the softmax algorithm only reads shared_max[0] after the max reduction completes (to get row_max), and this location at shared_mem[0] is never overwritten by shared_sum writes (which start at shared_mem[1]). The sum reduction operates on contiguous memory shared_mem[1..256] and correctly produces the sum in shared_sum[0]=shared_mem[1]. All __syncthreads() barriers ensure proper ordering between phases. The mutation is semantically equivalent under the fixed 1D block launch configuration.
rounds.kill_strategy: Unkillable - the mutant is semantically equivalent. With blockDim.y=1, the memory overlap between shared_max and shared_sum is harmless because only shared_max[0] is needed after the max phase, and it's preserved at shared_mem[0] which shared_sum never touches.
rounds.recommendations: When testing shared memory offset mutations, verify whether the algorithm's data flow actually requires the non-overlapping regions. In this case, the parallel reduction pattern only needs the final result at index 0, making the rest of the array disposable after each phase - a subtle equivalence that value testing cannot expose.
